manufacturer.amstrad.description: British manufacturer whose low-cost IBM-compatible PCs combined compact industrial design with model-specific firmware and peripherals.
manufacturer.amstrad.history:
Amstrad began in London in 1968 as A. M. S. Trading, founded by Alan Sugar. It first sold and then made affordable consumer electronics: price, compact design and mass distribution were features of the company before it built computers.

The 1984 CPC464 brought that strategy into the home. Its CPC family combined computer, keyboard and tape or disk drive with a monitor that also housed the power supply. The 1985 PCW8256 took a different path: it was a package centred on writing and office work. They were not two versions of one computer, but different answers for home and text users.

In 1985 Amstrad acquired from Clive Sinclair the worldwide rights to sell and manufacture Sinclair computer products and their intellectual property. It continued the Spectrum commercially, but the purchase does not turn earlier Sinclair models into Amstrad designs. The following year, the PC1512 opened a third branch: an IBM-compatible computer with MS-DOS, sold as a lower-cost office-PC alternative. Its successors coexisted with CPC, PCW and Spectrum because they served different markets and software.

From 1988 the brand also made satellite-television equipment. The company was broken up in 1997, and the company retaining the name was acquired by BSkyB in 2007. Its computing period makes one point clear: Amstrad did not follow one architecture, but made very different families accessible to particular audiences.
